Let \(q_1 = 5 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{C}\) sit at A and \(q_2 = -3 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{C}\) at B, with \(AB = 16\,\text{cm} = 0.16\,\text{m}\). Potential is a scalar, so the total potential at a point distant \(x\) from A on the line AB is the algebraic sum of the two contributions, and we set it to zero.

Case 1 — a point BETWEEN the charges, so its distance from B is \((0.16 - x)\):

\(\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[\frac{q_1}{x} + \frac{q_2}{0.16 - x}\right] = 0 \Rightarrow \frac{5 \times 10^{-8}}{x} = \frac{3 \times 10^{-8}}{0.16 - x}\)

\(5(0.16 - x) = 3x \Rightarrow 0.80 = 8x \Rightarrow x = 0.10\,\text{m} = 10\,\text{cm}\)

Case 2 — a point BEYOND the negative charge, so its distance from B is \((x - 0.16)\):

\(\frac{5 \times 10^{-8}}{x} = \frac{3 \times 10^{-8}}{x - 0.16} \Rightarrow 5(x - 0.16) = 3x \Rightarrow 2x = 0.80 \Rightarrow x = 0.40\,\text{m} = 40\,\text{cm}\)

Case 3 — a point beyond the POSITIVE charge would need \(5(x + 0.16) = 3x\), giving \(x = -0.40\,\text{m}\), which is inadmissible. There is no null point on that side because the charge nearer to it is the larger one in magnitude.

The electric potential is zero at two points on the line joining the charges: at \(10\,\text{cm}\) from the \(5 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{C}\) charge (i.e. between the two charges), and at \(40\,\text{cm}\) from it on the side of the negative charge (i.e. \(24\,\text{cm}\) beyond the negative charge).

A regular hexagon is made up of six equilateral triangles meeting at its centre, so the distance from the centre to each vertex equals the side:

\(r = a = 10\,\text{cm} = 0.10\,\text{m}\)

Potential is a scalar, so the six equal charges \(q = 5\,\mu\text{C} = 5 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{C}\) simply add (no vector resolution is needed):

\(V = 6 \times \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q}{r} = 6 \times \left(9 \times 10^{9}\,\text{N m}^{2}\,\text{C}^{-2}\right) \times \frac{5 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{C}}{0.10\,\text{m}}\)

\(V = 6 \times 4.5 \times 10^{5}\,\text{V}\)

Potential at the centre of the hexagon, \(V = 2.7 \times 10^{6}\,\text{V}\).

The two charges are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign, \(q = 2\,\mu\text{C}\) at A and \(-q\) at B.

(a) Consider any point P that is equidistant from A and B, say \(AP = BP = r\). The potential there is

\(V = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[\frac{q}{r} + \frac{-q}{r}\right] = 0\)

The set of all points equidistant from A and B is the plane that is perpendicular to AB and passes through its mid-point. Every point of that plane has zero potential, so it is an equipotential surface of the system.

(b) The electric field is always perpendicular to an equipotential surface (any component along the surface would do work in moving a charge between two points at the same potential, which is impossible). Hence at every point of this plane \(\mathbf{E}\) is normal to the plane. Its sense is from the positive charge towards the negative charge, i.e. along the direction A to B.

(a) The plane perpendicular to AB through its mid-point, on which the potential is zero everywhere.
(b) Normal to that plane, directed along AB (from the positive charge to the negative charge).

For a charged conductor in electrostatic equilibrium the excess charge resides entirely on the outer surface, and outside it the sphere behaves as though its whole charge were concentrated at the centre.

Given \(R = 12\,\text{cm} = 0.12\,\text{m}\) and \(Q = 1.6 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{C}\).

(a) A Gaussian sphere drawn anywhere inside the conductor encloses no charge, so by Gauss's law the flux and hence the field is zero. (This is also required for equilibrium: a non-zero field would drive the free charges.)

\(E = 0\)

(b) Just outside the surface, taking \(r = R\):

\(E = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q}{R^{2}} = \frac{\left(9 \times 10^{9}\,\text{N m}^{2}\,\text{C}^{-2}\right)\left(1.6 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{C}\right)}{(0.12\,\text{m})^{2}} = \frac{1.44 \times 10^{3}}{1.44 \times 10^{-2}}\,\text{N C}^{-1}\)

\(E = 1.0 \times 10^{5}\,\text{N C}^{-1}\), directed radially outward.

(c) At \(r = 18\,\text{cm} = 0.18\,\text{m}\), which is outside the sphere:

\(E = \frac{\left(9 \times 10^{9}\right)\left(1.6 \times 10^{-7}\right)}{(0.18)^{2}} = \frac{1.44 \times 10^{3}}{3.24 \times 10^{-2}}\,\text{N C}^{-1}\)

\(E = 4.4 \times 10^{4}\,\text{N C}^{-1}\), directed radially outward.

(a) \(E = 0\)
(b) \(E = 1.0 \times 10^{5}\,\text{N C}^{-1}\), radially outward
(c) \(E = 4.4 \times 10^{4}\,\text{N C}^{-1}\), radially outward

For a parallel plate capacitor with air (effectively vacuum) between the plates,

\(C = \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d} = 8\,\text{pF}\)

The plate area \(A\) is unchanged. The separation becomes \(d' = d/2\) and the gap is filled with a dielectric of constant \(K = 6\), so

\(C' = \frac{K\varepsilon_0 A}{d'} = \frac{K\varepsilon_0 A}{d/2} = 2K\left(\frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}\right) = 2K C\)

\(C' = 2 \times 6 \times 8\,\text{pF}\)

The capacitance becomes \(C' = 96\,\text{pF}\) (twelve times its original value).

Three identical capacitors, \(C_1 = C_2 = C_3 = 9\,\text{pF}\), in series.

(a) For a series combination the reciprocals add:

\(\frac{1}{C} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2} + \frac{1}{C_3} = \frac{3}{9\,\text{pF}} = \frac{1}{3\,\text{pF}}\)

\(C = 3\,\text{pF}\)

(b) In a series combination every capacitor carries the same charge

\(Q = CV = \left(3 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{F}\right)\left(120\,\text{V}\right) = 3.6 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{C}\)

so the potential difference across each is

\(V_1 = \frac{Q}{C_1} = \frac{3.6 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{C}}{9 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{F}} = 40\,\text{V}\)

Since the three capacitors are identical the \(120\,\text{V}\) simply divides equally between them.

(a) Total capacitance \(C = 3\,\text{pF}\)
(b) Potential difference across each capacitor \(= 40\,\text{V}\)

Three capacitors \(C_1 = 2\,\text{pF}\), \(C_2 = 3\,\text{pF}\), \(C_3 = 4\,\text{pF}\) in parallel.

(a) For a parallel combination the capacitances add:

\(C = C_1 + C_2 + C_3 = (2 + 3 + 4)\,\text{pF}\)

\(C = 9\,\text{pF}\)

(b) In a parallel combination every capacitor has the SAME potential difference across it, \(V = 100\,\text{V}\), so \(Q = CV\) for each:

\(Q_1 = \left(2 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{F}\right)\left(100\,\text{V}\right) = 2 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{C}\)

\(Q_2 = \left(3 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{F}\right)\left(100\,\text{V}\right) = 3 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{C}\)

\(Q_3 = \left(4 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{F}\right)\left(100\,\text{V}\right) = 4 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{C}\)

As a check, the total charge \(9 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{C}\) equals \(CV = 9\,\text{pF} \times 100\,\text{V}\).

(a) Total capacitance \(C = 9\,\text{pF}\)
(b) \(Q_1 = 2 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{C}\), \(Q_2 = 3 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{C}\), \(Q_3 = 4 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{C}\)

Convert to SI: \(A = 6 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}^{2}\) is already in SI, and \(d = 3\,\text{mm} = 3 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}\).

For a parallel plate capacitor with air between the plates,

\(C = \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d} = \frac{\left(8.854 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{F m}^{-1}\right)\left(6 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}^{2}\right)}{3 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}}\)

\(C = 8.854 \times 10^{-12} \times 2\,\text{F} = 1.77 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{F} \approx 18\,\text{pF}\)

With the capacitor connected to \(V = 100\,\text{V}\), the charge on each plate is

\(Q = CV = \left(1.77 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{F}\right)\left(100\,\text{V}\right)\)

Capacitance \(C \approx 18\,\text{pF}\) \(\left(1.77 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{F}\right)\), and the charge on each plate \(Q \approx 1.8 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{C}\) (equal and opposite on the two plates).

From Exercise 2.8 the air capacitor has \(C = 18\,\text{pF}\) and, at \(100\,\text{V}\), carries \(Q = 1.8 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{C}\). The mica sheet is \(3\,\text{mm}\) thick, exactly the plate separation, so it FILLS the gap completely and the capacitance everywhere becomes

\(C' = K C = 6 \times 18\,\text{pF} = 108\,\text{pF}\)

(a) With the supply still connected the potential difference is held fixed at \(V = 100\,\text{V}\). The capacitance rises six-fold, so the charge must rise six-fold too:

\(Q' = C'V = \left(108 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{F}\right)\left(100\,\text{V}\right) = 1.08 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{C}\)

The extra charge is drawn from the battery; the voltage is unchanged.

(b) With the supply disconnected the plates are isolated, so the CHARGE is what stays fixed at \(Q = 1.8 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{C}\). The potential difference therefore falls:

\(V' = \frac{Q}{C'} = \frac{CV}{KC} = \frac{V}{K} = \frac{100\,\text{V}}{6} = 16.7\,\text{V}\)

Physically the polarised mica sets up an opposing field that reduces the net field between the plates by the factor \(K\), and hence reduces the potential difference by the same factor.

(a) Supply connected: \(V = 100\,\text{V}\) (unchanged), \(C' = 108\,\text{pF}\), \(Q' = 1.08 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{C}\).
(b) Supply disconnected: \(Q = 1.8 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{C}\) (unchanged), \(C' = 108\,\text{pF}\), \(V' = 16.7\,\text{V}\).

The energy stored in a charged capacitor is

\(U = \tfrac{1}{2}CV^{2}\)

with \(C = 12\,\text{pF} = 12 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{F}\) and \(V = 50\,\text{V}\):

\(U = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(12 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{F}\right)\left(50\,\text{V}\right)^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(12 \times 10^{-12}\right)\left(2.5 \times 10^{3}\right)\,\text{J}\)

Electrostatic energy stored, \(U = 1.5 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{J}\).

Initially \(C_1 = 600\,\text{pF} = 6 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{F}\) is charged to \(V = 200\,\text{V}\).

Initial stored energy:

\(U_i = \tfrac{1}{2}C_1V^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(6 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{F}\right)\left(200\,\text{V}\right)^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(6 \times 10^{-10}\right)\left(4 \times 10^{4}\right) = 1.2 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{J}\)

Charge on it:

\(Q = C_1V = \left(6 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{F}\right)\left(200\,\text{V}\right) = 1.2 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{C}\)

Once the supply is removed and the second, uncharged \(600\,\text{pF}\) capacitor is connected, the two are in parallel and the total charge is conserved:

\(C_{\text{total}} = 600 + 600 = 1200\,\text{pF} = 1.2 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{F}\)

\(V' = \frac{Q}{C_{\text{total}}} = \frac{1.2 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{C}}{1.2 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{F}} = 100\,\text{V}\)

Final stored energy:

\(U_f = \tfrac{1}{2}C_{\text{total}}V'^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(1.2 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{F}\right)\left(100\,\text{V}\right)^{2} = 6 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{J}\)

The missing energy is not destroyed: while the charge redistributes a transient current flows between the capacitors, and that energy is dissipated as heat in the connecting wires and radiated away as electromagnetic radiation.

Energy lost, \(U_i - U_f = 1.2 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{J} - 6 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{J} = 6 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{J}\) (half the initial energy).
